title: From sand to switch
summary: Why silicon can switch: band gaps, doping, p–n junctions, growing a perfect crystal and implanting dopants.

challenges.title: Grow a perfect crystal
challenges.task: Pull a dislocation-free 300 mm ingot and taper it off safely.

learn.plain: Silicon is a material that conducts electricity only a little. Adding a pinch of other atoms decides whether it carries negative or positive charges, and a voltage on a nearby gate can switch it between conducting and not. Everything starts with a crystal so perfect that every atom is in its place.
learn.engineer: Intrinsic carrier density n_i ≈ 10¹⁰ cm⁻³ at 300 K follows exp(−E_g/2kT); doping from 10¹⁵ to 10²⁰ cm⁻³ sets majority carriers with n·p = n_i². Junction physics: V_bi = (kT/q)·ln(N_A·N_D/n_i²), depletion width ∝ √((V_bi − V)/N). Czochralski growth uses Dash necking to eliminate dislocations, with diameter controlled by pull rate and melt temperature; oxygen from the quartz crucible (~10¹⁸ cm⁻³) aids gettering. Implant profiles follow projected range R_p and straggle ΔR_p; spike, flash and laser anneals trade activation against diffusion.

quiz.q: Why does adding a few phosphorus atoms make silicon conduct much better?
options: Each phosphorus atom brings one spare electron that is free to move
quiz.why: Phosphorus has five outer electrons; silicon bonds need four, so one is free. That makes n-type silicon.

quiz.q: What does forward bias do to a p–n junction?
options: Widens the depletion region and blocks current
Shrinks the depletion region so current flows
Turns it into a capacitor only
quiz.why: Above about 0.6 V forward, current rises steeply. Reverse bias widens the depletion region instead.

quiz.q: Why is a thin "neck" pulled at the start of crystal growth?
options: So dislocations from the seed grow out and vanish before the crystal widens
To make the ingot look nicer
quiz.why: This Dash necking technique is why commercial silicon crystals are dislocation-free.
